slides.title: Word forms
slides.body:
thrill
(noun / verb)
slides.notes: Step 1: Show base word 'thrill'. Ask: What does thrill mean? An exciting feeling.

slides.title: thrill → thrilling
slides.body:
thrilling
"She starred in a thrilling movie called Spider-Man."
When a verb (thrill) describes a noun, it becomes an adjective: thrill → thrilling
slides.notes: Step 2: Show how 'thrill' becomes 'thrilling' to describe the movie. The -ing suffix turns a verb into an adjective. Show Kirsten Dunst (from Spider-Man). Ask students to find other examples in the exercise.

slides.title: Structured Discourse
slides.body:
**1. Opinion** — What do you think?

**2. Reason** — Why do you think that?

**3. Story** — Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?
slides.notes: Explain: When you speak for a minute, follow this structure. Opinion → Reason → Story/Example. We'll practice with Ex 2, Q1.

slides.title: Model — Ex 2, Q1
slides.body: I think a good screenplay is more important than a good soundtrack. Why? Because the story is what makes us care about the characters. For example, in Titanic, the screenplay makes us fall in love with Jack and Rose. We feel their happiness and their sadness. Without a good story, even beautiful music means nothing. Another example is Inception — it has a very complex plot, but the screenplay makes it easy to follow. We care about Cobb and we want him to succeed. I also love The Dark Knight. The screenplay is so well written that we understand why the Joker does what he does. We don't agree with him, but we understand him. That's what a good screenplay does — it makes us think and feel. A soundtrack can add emotion, but it can't create the story. The story comes first every time. So next time you watch a movie, pay attention to the screenplay. Is the story well told? Does it make you care? If yes, then the screenplay is doing its job.
slides.notes: Play the audio model (currently 30s — regenerate for 60s when Inworld credits are available). Point out the natural structure: Opinion → Reason → Example → Another example → Conclusion.

slides.title: Questions?
slides.body: Any questions about what we've learned today?
slides.notes: Wrap up. Ask: What new words can you use to talk about movies? What's the difference between a documentary and a fictional film?
